mcqs.question: Why is a calling convention necessary when a library is compiled by a different compiler than the code that calls it?
options: Because compilers always produce incompatible machine code regardless of convention
Because both sides need to agree on where arguments and return values go, or the call would misinterpret memory/registers
Because calling conventions only matter for interpreted languages, not compiled ones
Because the CPU enforces a single universal calling convention in hardware
mcqs.explanation: A calling convention is the shared agreement that makes independently-compiled code interoperate correctly. Compilers aren't inherently incompatible if they honor the same convention, this is a compiled-language concern (part of the ABI) even more than interpreted ones, and hardware itself doesn't enforce a specific convention — it's a software-level agreement.

mcqs.question: Why does taking the address of a local variable and using it after the function returns cause undefined behavior?
options: Local variables are always stored in read-only memory
The stack frame containing that variable is torn down when the function returns, so the memory is no longer reserved for it
Local variables are automatically copied to the heap on function exit
It's actually always safe as long as no other function is called afterward
mcqs.explanation: The frame is deallocated on return, so the memory can be reused by the next call — reading it afterward is reading stale, unreserved memory. Locals aren't read-only or auto-copied to the heap, and the behavior is undefined regardless of whether another function is called next.

mcqs.question: If a function uses a callee-saved register internally, what must it do before returning?
options: Nothing — callee-saved registers can be left in any state
Restore the register to the value it had when the function was entered
Zero out the register for security reasons
Save it to the heap for the caller to retrieve later
mcqs.explanation: Callee-saved means the callee is responsible for preserving that register's value across the call, restoring it before returning. Leaving it modified breaks the caller's assumptions, zeroing isn't the convention's requirement, and there's no heap-save mechanism involved.

mcqs.question: What is the purpose of a function's prologue?
options: To execute the function's return value computation
To set up the new stack frame — saving the caller's frame pointer and reserving space for locals
To restore registers before jumping back to the caller
To validate the function's arguments against a type schema
mcqs.explanation: The prologue establishes the frame (save old frame pointer, set new one, reserve local space) before the function body runs. Restoring registers before returning is the epilogue's job, return-value computation is part of the function body, and there's no runtime type-schema validation involved.

mcqs.question: Why does unbounded recursion eventually cause a stack overflow?
options: Because recursive functions leak memory on the heap
Because each recursive call allocates its own stack frame, and frames keep accumulating until the stack's memory region is exhausted
Because the CPU limits functions to a fixed number of calls per program
Because return addresses get overwritten by earlier recursive calls
mcqs.explanation: Each call pushes a new frame; without a base case ending recursion, frames pile up and eventually exceed the reserved stack region. This is a stack (not heap) memory issue, there's no CPU-enforced call-count limit, and correctly implemented recursion doesn't overwrite earlier return addresses — each frame is independent.

mcqs.question: Why is an unchecked buffer overflow into a local array on the stack potentially more dangerous than just corrupting other locals?
options: It can overwrite the saved return address, letting an attacker redirect execution when the function returns
It always crashes the program immediately, which is the worst-case outcome
It can only corrupt data, never affect control flow
Local arrays are stored separately from the return address, so overflow can never reach it
mcqs.explanation: Locals commonly sit below the saved return address in memory, so an overflow can walk past them and corrupt the return address itself, hijacking control flow. An immediate crash isn't guaranteed (attackers specifically avoid crashing when exploiting this), it very much can affect control flow, and locals and the return address do share the same stack region.
